text: Encryption is only as strong as its key management, and that's literal, not just a slogan. All of Lesson 20's cryptography is useless if the key itself is mishandled, stored next to the data it protects, never rotated, known by too many people, or lost entirely.

Every key goes through four stages. Generate, created with enough randomness that it can't be guessed. Distribute, gotten to the systems that need it without being exposed in transit, email and shared spreadsheets are common real mistakes. Rotate, replaced periodically so an undetected compromise has a limited exposure window instead of a permanent one. Retire, properly destroyed or archived when no longer needed, while still allowing old backups to be decrypted if retention policy requires it. Skipping rotation is the single most common real-world gap.

Last lesson's TDE chain, a master key protecting a certificate, protecting a database encryption key, is a real-world instance of a general pattern. A key-encrypting key protects a data-encrypting key, rather than one key doing everything. The DEK does the actual high-volume work of encrypting data. The KEK's only job is protecting the DEK, and because it's used far less often, it can live somewhere more tightly controlled without becoming a bottleneck. Rotating the DEK is also far cheaper than re-encrypting everything from scratch.

A hardware security module is a tamper-resistant device built to generate, store, and use keys without the key material ever leaving the device in plaintext. Operations get sent to the HSM instead of exporting the key. And who holds a key is itself a segregation-of-duties question, a key custodian who can also access the data it protects has effectively unrestricted plaintext access, so mature programs split key-lifecycle responsibility from the people who query the encrypted data day to day.

That closes the protection techniques this chapter covers, masking, tokenization, encryption, and the key management underneath it. Next up: row and column security, controlling what a query returns before encryption even enters the picture.
